method: Sidereal time is the hour angle of the vernal equinox: the right ascension standing on a meridian, so whatever shares that right ascension is at its highest. The page follows the U.S. Naval Observatory's approximate algorithm. The UTC date and time become Julian dates through integer day-number arithmetic, so the day's 0 h Julian date JD0 (ending in .5) and the hours H elapsed since midnight are exact. With D = JD0 - 2451545.0 and T the centuries from J2000.0, Greenwich mean sidereal time is 6.697375 + 0.065709824279 D + 1.0027379 H + 0.0000258 T squared hours, reduced modulo 24. The equation of the equinoxes is the nutation in longitude times the cosine of the obliquity, with dpsi = -0.000319 sin(Omega) - 0.000024 sin(2L) hours and Omega = 125.04 - 0.052954 D, L = 280.47 + 0.98565 D, epsilon = 23.4393 - 0.0000004 D degrees; adding it turns mean into apparent sidereal time. East longitude divided by 15 shifts either figure to the local meridian, so western longitudes are negative and the value wraps through zero. An optional right ascension is subtracted from local apparent sidereal time to give the hour angle, folded into -12 to +12 hours: negative when the target is still east of the meridian, which is also the sidereal interval until it transits, positive once it has crossed. Times print as hh:mm:ss.ss, rounded to the nearest hundredth of a second and carried into minutes, hours and around midnight; right ascension on the meridian prints to four decimal degrees. The input is UTC: UT1 and UTC differ by at most 0.9 s and the Observatory quotes 0.432 s maximum error for 2000-2100 with UT1, so the seconds are good to about one second. Dates are accepted from 1800 to 2100, real calendar days only, with times from 00:00 to 23:59:59, longitudes from -180 to 180 degrees and right ascensions from 0 up to but not including 24 hours. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.
